Historical identity / living descendants

Jumano

Spanish and later sources used “Jumano” for peoples across Texas, New Mexico, and adjacent northern Mexico. Scholars disagree whether it named one distinct people, several groups, or a broader label; contemporary Jumano community accounts describe living descendants. This profile keeps historical classifications and present-day community identity separate.

Names & relationshipsThe historical label Jumano appears in sources for different peoples and settings. This entry also links to contemporary Jumano community accounts and a separate Indigenous-led La Junta organization that names Jumano among several descendant communities. These relationships are presented with their own source scope; they do not establish that every historical use names one polity, or that one modern organization represents everyone connected to the name.

01

A historical name with contested scope

Historical materials used “Jumano” across more than one region and context. Nancy P. Hickerson’s distinct-trading-people interpretation appears in both her Handbook of Texas article and later scholarship, while older and other scholarly models proposed a broad Spanish label or linguistic connections to different peoples. Studies also disagree about whether particular Jumano groups were distinct from, related to, or interdependent with settled Patarabueye communities at La Junta. The Texas Beyond History exhibit and Bradley Folsom’s regional summary describe trade and mutual dependence while retaining cultural distinctions; these interpretations draw on inconsistent colonial names and should not be collapsed into one settled identity for every group. A National Park Service visitor page describes Gran Quivira at its peak as home to “eastern Tompiro/Jumano people” and as a Plains–Pueblo crossroads. Because this short public-history page gives no underlying citations and uses a combined label, it is useful evidence of a modern institutional summary, not proof that Tompiro and Jumano were interchangeable.

02

Trade, diplomacy, and a changing borderlands

Historical syntheses describe Jumano travel and trade linking the South Plains, lower Pecos, Rio Grande, New Mexico, and communities farther east. They report exchanges with Pueblo, La Junta, and Caddo communities and diplomacy associated with Juan Sabeata. Robert Weddle’s biography of Juan Domínguez de Mendoza describes Sabeata’s appeal and the 1683–84 expedition; route reconstructions and the proposed location of San Clemente remain disputed. The accounts were produced in colonial settings, and their place names, population figures, and ethnic labels require attribution rather than treatment as settled facts.

03

La Junta was a crossroads, not a single people

La Junta de los Ríos, near the Río Conchos–Río Grande confluence, was a region of settled villages and movement among different communities. The Texas Beyond History exhibit distinguishes villagers described by Spanish sources as Conchos, Patarabueyes, or Amotomancos from Jumano traders and visitors, and explains how translation and later illustrations have sometimes blurred those categories. Bradley Folsom’s regional article presents a later interpretation of Jumano and Patarabueye communities as mutually dependent while culturally distinct. These are interpretations of incomplete written records and archaeological evidence; the confluence should not be assigned to a single people.

04

What the colonial record can—and cannot—show

Most historical works in this collection rely on Spanish colonial documents, translated accounts, or later scholarly syntheses. Such sources describe encounters, trade, missions, and conflict, but they were written by outsiders and use names inconsistently. Two Arizona Historical Indexes records dated August and October 1683 identify correspondence involving Jumanes, Shulimes, and Sabeata and point to archival volumes and translation files. The catalogue summaries are not the letters: the original documents and translations remain unread, so no claims in those summaries are treated as independently verified here. The 1683–84 Mendoza diary is likewise represented by scholarly summaries and a catalogue record, not a direct reading of the manuscript.

05

Living communities and contemporary accounts

A 2021 local newspaper report records Jumano Nation of Texas historian Felix Bonilla Salmeron describing the nation’s effort to connect with descendants and rejecting the claim that Jumano people disappeared. This is a dated, attributed community perspective reported by a journalist, not a census or an independently verified genealogy. Separately, the Indigenous-led People of La Junta for Preservation describes its descendant communities as including Jumano, Julime, Chisos, Concho, Lipan Apache, and others, and explains its stewardship work at La Junta. That organization’s broader community scope is not interchangeable with the Jumano Nation of Texas.

Read the sources [7] Big Bend Sentinel [8] People of La Junta for Preservation [12] Humanities Texas

06

Reading claims about disappearance and recognition

Some scholarly summaries say the colonial record stopped identifying Jumano as a distinct people or that their trade networks and political position changed by the eighteenth century. That describes an interpretation of surviving documents, not proof that descendants or living communities disappeared. Contemporary accounts from Jumano Nation of Texas and the separate Indigenous-led People of La Junta for Preservation have their own stated scope and are not interchangeable. Texas House Resolution 1565 is a state expression honoring the Jumano Indian Nation of Texas; its historical assertions and population claim are not independently verified here and it is not a federal recognition decision.

A substantial scholarly state-history synthesis with a bibliography. The Jumano Indians in Texas, 1650–1771 ↗

A full, early scholarly article arguing that Jumano groups remained in southern Texas into the eighteenth century and that the name was also applied to Taovayas/Wichita people. Read as a dated intervention in an identity debate, not current consensus. The article contains OCR errors and relies on colonial documents; cited manuscript originals were not inspected.

Inspection scope: The complete 26-page scan was inspected across the introduction, Nueces geography, 1683–1716 records, Apache alliances, and the 1771 Taovayas discussion. Original manuscript sources and other works Bolton cites were not inspected.
